Mr. Speaker, commenting on Bill C-91 today I have a number of points I wish to make, many of them pertaining to financial management or mismanagement thereof. Bill C-91 is an act to amend the Financial Administration Act and other acts in consequence thereof. If the average lay person is to read the contents of a bill of that nature and size, all I say is thank goodness for good researchers and advisers in this business.
Many of the improvements that are listed here have been recommended by public accounts committees over the years of their sittings in this House. A number of those have been accomplished recently by our public accounts committee. For example, there is the addition of sovereign loans that are unlikely to be paid are added to the national debt of Canada. Before they were just sitting there. Everybody knew that we would never collect many of those debts from foreign countries. It is a good move to bring those into the financial structure of the countiy, showing them as a national debt because undoubtedly we are going to have to cover them at some time in the future anyway. That has been a good move. It is one that the Auditor General has wanted for some time.
I have many comments that I want to make about this bill. While it brings out all the good points of government, we do not want it to be a cushion for the government to be spreading what it considers to be its good news and its updates and so on without also bringing in the basic and broad underlying weaknesses of financial management in Canada today. This bill is an act to amend the Financial Administration Act. It is a housekeeping bill in many ways on matters of a technical nature that have been evolving for the last five years in financial management and control practices of the government, recommended on many occasions by the Auditor General and the public accounts committee.
Many of these amendments are being made on recommendations of those two bodies. I congratulate the Auditor General on his very constructive remarks over the past number of years. I know that when you are in government you do not like the reports of auditors general sometimes. I sat on that side of the House for a number of years and I know what it feels like. It is very necessary in government to have a good auditor general and a good staff behind him. I think we are well served by the auditor general's organization, from all members of
his staff and the way they serve the House of Commons of Canada.
There is nothing inherently wrong with this bill. As I said, it is a housekeeping bill. It is in most cases merely legitimizing into legislation the things that are current practice anyway. Therefore, the Liberal approach to this is that we are quite happy to see these changes formalized, but there have been many areas of mismanagement on the part of this government and it has no reason to pat itself on the back.
The public debt has doubled in five years from $170 billion to $351 billion. The scary part of it is that in spite of all the increases in taxes and the rhetoric of this government, we are now on our way to tripling the national debt in this country. That is a very scary thing indeed.
The government missed the opportunity to make meaningful reductions in the deficit during five years of world-wide economic growth. This government had five years of the best economic growth in the country. Even at that, the deficit and the national debt in this country continued to grow by leaps and bounds. Yet they campaigned in 1984 by telling all Canadians how simple it was going to be to bring the national debt of Canada under control. They have succeeded in their six years in power in increasing the national debt in this country by more than it has been increased in any period of time since Confederation. Not much of a record to be proud of, Mr. Speaker.
The deficit is increasing, not decreasing as the government would have us believe. Let us take a look at the figures. The deficit has risen from $28.1 billion in 1987-88 to $28.7 billion in 1988-1989 and to $30.5 billion in 1989-90. Many efforts have been made to save the face of the finance minister. This is about the third major round of cutting the Public Service of Canada and there is a feeling out there that when they do that, they are hitting Ottawa and area.
Just to clarify that point, I want to say that three out of four public servants in Canada live outside the National Capital Region. They are spread all the way across this country from Halifax to the west coast and from the south of Canada to the Arctic circle. It is very easy to attack public servants because they cannot stand up and defend themselves.
November 26, 1990

When you attack the Public Service, decrease the numbers of the Public Service, you can go around to those who believe that that is a great thing. You brag about it and say: "What a great fellow am I". Then they turn around and hire contractors to do much of the same work that public servants were doing before. They say: "We are saving money by doing this". Well, Mr. Speaker, just a few weeks ago we had the Treasury Board, the Privy Council and the Auditor General before the public accounts committee. I asked them specifically for a comparison of the costs of contracting out as opposed to the amount it would cost had those public servants been retained. They said: "Oh, yes, we can get you those figures."
It was not very long until I got a reply from them to the opposite. This is what Treasury Board had to say: "In connection with the information requested on personal services contracts which replace the use of public servants, the Treasury Board Secretariat does not collect such data. As far as we are aware, departments have not been gathering statistical data of that kind. We do not have data on what portion of the contract statistics that have been collected per the paragraph above would have replaced the use of public servants. Furthermore, our statistics would not likely incorporate all contracting out of services but only those captured by the criteria of the two special areas of interest."
On what grounds does any member of this government go around Canada saying: "We have decreased the Public Service from such a figure down to such a figure and boy, are we doing a good job." They say by contracting out they are saving money. Yet, they do not have any statistics to prove their point. That is just a bunch of rhetoric. It is really amazing what you find out. You are promised information. Then you find they do not have it.
When you cut the Public Service, you are not only downsizing the Public Service. You are downsizing the morale as well because people do not know when the hatchet is going to fall on them. This is not the way to get the best work out of your employees. The Public Service of Canada has been the scapegoat of this government on many occasions. This government is going to pay dearly for those attacks.
Government Orders
Federal tax revenues have increased by $50 billion since 1984. This government has increased its tax revenues by $50 billion since it gained power six years ago. The finance minister has had more than enough tax increases to reduce the deficit, but he has failed to do so.
Because of high interest rates, the deficit will be $4 billion to $6 billion higher in 1990-91, unless the government takes additional action to raise taxes or cut spending. It is after everybody to impress upon them how important it is that it cuts the deficit and how important it is to downsize the national debt. It then turns around and brings in a high interest rate policy that results in adding $4 billion to $6 billion to the national debt of this country. It then brags about its great success in financial management.
The high interest rate policy is keeping interest rates in Canada more than 4 per cent higher than they are in the United States. A public debt of $351 billion is equivalent to a personal debt of $25,000 for each Canadian taxpayer. Each Canadian must now pay $2,500 in taxes each year just to pay the interest on the federal government's debt. The government is on its way to tripling the national debt, and it has only been in power for six years.
The proportion of the debt owed to foreigners-and this is a crucial point that many Canadians will not take any heart in-has doubled under the Conservative government, from 10 per cent to 20 per cent. Before these people came to power, 90 per cent of the national debt was owned by Canadians and interest rates were being paid to those Canadians. Now, there is another 20 per cent being paid outside the country.
High interest rates have caused Japanese and European investors to purchase Government of Canada securities. This means that more of Canada's future wealth will have to be paid to foreigners in interest, and the government calls this good financial management.
The Conservative policy has been to shift its deficit systematically to the provinces and to other levels of government. This is a serious situation. You are not cutting anything in Canada when you simply shift your problems over to another level of government.
Cuts to transfer payments to the provinces for health care and post-secondary education squeeze provincial budgets. Cuts to unemployment insurance push more people on to welfare, which costs the provinces and the municipalities more money. Federal spending cuts even-

Government Orders
tually result in higher provincial taxes and higher municipal property taxes.
When people across Canada have a major increase in their municipal taxes and an increase in their provincial taxes, it may well be due to the fact that the federal government is unloading more of its debt and more of its administrative difficulties on to the provinces and on to municipalities in order to try to make itself look good.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take the opportunity to speak to this bill because I think that this particular piece of legislation is much more important than has been indicated and is much more than bare housekeeping. Within this bill is the expanding of authority or power, giving it to the Treasury Board, taking it from other ministers and other acts. It is put into the area of an Order in Council and regulations under the Treasury Board.
When the minister let slip that this was going to be one of the pieces of legislation that was going to help to eliminate the deficit, he really meant that, because within this particular piece of legislation is the authority for Treasury Board to define what is a service. There is no definition of a service or a facility in the bill.
If that is looked at a little more deeply, it will be found that that can mean a considerable amount more than would appear on the surface. The umbrella legislation is the Financial Administration Act. It affects every department and ever}' movement of funds between departments. It is umbrella legislation under which the government is supposed to be able to control the financial structure of its operations.
If the operations which are presently the responsibility of every one of the departments are centralized under the Treasury Board, and the government decides it wants a 15 per cent or a 20 per cent increase, it can do it right across the board without any problem at all. It does not have to go to each minister or act to get the authority under that act to change the regulations because it can now be done centrally.
I think that is the danger of this particular piece of legislation. It puts into the hands of the Treasury Board and the cabinet much more power than they have had in the past. It is the kind of power which allows them to fleece the citizens of Canada without coming to Parliament, or without going to the department which knows the most about the particular charges that are being made. It gives the Treasury Board the authority to define what a service is and how much should be charged for it.

What the Act did was enable the government to charge fees in a broader category of users of radio
licences. The minister, at the time, assured this House that these additional charges would only apply to provincial and federal government agencies. They would not apply, for example, to municipalities that have radio licences for their use for local police protection, search and rescue, fire protection, emergency measures and they would also not apply to voluntary agencies, agencies like fire departments which are comprised of volunteers and perform the same types of services on a voluntary basis often over a wide area and for which there are no charges for these services.

This regulatory change, which was permitted one month of pre-publication through the Canada Gazette, is a most arcane and complex piece of regulation, combined with a schedule which would require a whole company of accountants a month to figure out, let alone the fire departments that were affected. Of course, it went right by the voluntary fire departments that were most affected. They have discovered since then that they are now saddled with an enormous increase in their radio licence fees.

pay an additional $8,574 or $17,148 for their radio licence fees. They are unable to meet that charge.

On April 1, 1990, a new formula financing arrangement went into effect between the federal government and the government of the NWT. The immediate financial impact of the new arrangements is the reduction of the 1990-91 grant to the government of the Northwest Territories of about $25 million. Over the next five years, the reductions will amount to about $110 million. Not only are these cuts damaging to the NWT's fiscal position but the new formula contains serious flaws which will limit our ability to develop the northern economy.
It is particularly serious in that the Northwest Territories, at a time when the goods and services tax would definitely be an imposition and the high interest rate policy dominates all discussions on the economy, the new unemployment insurance bill, which definitely impacts the north because of the high seasonal employment situation that exists there, will have devastating effects on people in Canada's north.
Essentially it is to say that any kind of legislation that comes from the federal government definitely has an impact on the north in a disproportionate way than it does in any other region of Canada in that the ties are very close. Although we have an act that we are governed by, we definitely are still an extension and we still have these huge transfers that we have to adhere to strict regulations to manage these resources by.
Having said that, I guess we could assume that in the territories we have been virtually taken off the transportation grid. There have been major cutbacks which will have a very devastating effect on the north, in that the north has a very high cost of travel for its public. Essentially, most of the travel is by air and most of the
communities serviced are by air travel. There really is not the kind of infrastructure that exists in other parts of Canada.
As far as the communications grid is concerned, I guess essentially the million dollar cutbacks referred to in the budgetary cutbacks of a few days ago will definitely have an impact on the voice that the north has through this particular mechanism to communicate.
In terms of communications and the Financial Administration Act, I suppose the north would be in a position, as would every other community in the south, to be on an equal playing field in terms of its infrastructure, but the north lags behind.
In the last two months Gordon Wray, the Minister of Tourism and Economic Development for the Government of the Northwest Territories, stated in terms of a major transportation strategy he presented to his legislature: "Our transportation infrastructure lags far behind anywhere else in Canada and must be improved. Our lack of adequate roads, airports, docks and harbours handicaps our economic growth. A better transportation system will create opportunities for mining, tourism, fishing, trade and travel between communities".
This is a major concern of the territories. Finding the investment dollars for communities in the north would be a major consideration for this particular portfolio and this particular minister. It is of the utmost importance for this particular government to have the moneys to administer in a responsible way under the Financial Administration Act. It should be able to get returns instead of always playing catch-up and trying to build an infrastructure at the same time, which is degrading.
What I mean by that is that the strategy includes major program initiatives and a substantial financial commitment. The minister states that at current levels we would spend some $1.65 billion over the next 20 years on transportation. Achieving the four strategic objectives would require expenditures of $4.32 billion, representing an increase of $2.6 billion.
In the fiscal arrangement or the new formula financing arrangement that went into effect on April 1, 1990, it seems very hopeless to put forward any kind of an economic initiative for the north when we have the kinds of arrangements that are essentially going to degrade the future economic prospects of the north by $110 million over the next five years. The reality is that this is

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak for the second time today. After the break we had two weeks ago, I guess I thirsted for the battle. I am getting my fill today.
It is a good day to get up and speak on this bill, which is primarily a housekeeping bill. It enacts very technical changes and requirements to the Financial Administration Act. Before I start my speech, the hon. member opposite who just asked the last question, asked my colleague from Western Arctic a question. What he was looking for were some bouquets on the government's financial management ability of the fiscal resources of the nation. He might have been fishing in the wrong direction. I cannot say that this piece of legislation is bad. It is a technical piece of legislation. It tightens up some loopholes. There are a few things I find terribly wrong with it. I will deal with that because it reflects an error in policy direction that the government has taken.
The hon. member opposite asked my colleague from Western Arctic whether or not she thought that this government had made some modest steps towards proper financial accountability and proper management with the fiscal resources of the nation. I would like to put a case forward to prove that it is not just technical amendments to law that indicates what should be a benchmark of whether or not a government is fiscally managing itself properly, but other things like ACOA. ACOA is an agency that is not directly dealt with in this bill. The bill deals with Crown corporations and the like. I want to talk about ACOA and by doing so, perhaps I will answer my hon. colleague's question.
ACOA is a Crown corporation. It has a budget of $1.05 billion. When it was created, it was supposed to be new money. In a subsequent budget about a year ago, the
Minister of Finance indicated that in the area of fiscal responsibility, the government was going to extend the mandate of ACOA from five to seven years, which effectively is a 20 per cent cut. It could not get the word cut out of their lips, although everyone who looked at the amendments or the changes knew that it meant that Atlantic Canada, over that five-year period, would have 20 per cent less money to spend on economic development. Over and over, in my previous capacity as regional development critic and the critic for ACOA, I would ask the minister responsible for some accounting of how he and his officials were spending that $1.05 billion.
Repeatedly we got bafflegab and every type of distortion and diatribe so that the questions would not be answered.
Here is a case in point, a company called NSC Diesel. It was funded through ACOA. That is taxpayers' money. Do you want to talk about accountability? I asked the minister, many times, questions on NSC Diesel. Before it even got the superstructure up on its building, it went belly up and left dozens of small contractors on the eastern shore of Nova Scotia owed literally millions of dollars.
I could not get any answers from the government on financial accountability. I figured that since it was funded with public money and since it did not seem to have a market, the public had a right to know how that project got funded.
I had to go to the unusual length of asking the Auditor General, since the ministers on the front benches refused to answer. For goodness sakes, the government should have a look at whether or not this project was properly approved and whether or not there is some financial management accountability in the system.
In his report the Auditor General said that the project in question, which may end up costing taxpayers in this country over $10 million and probably cause the bankruptcy of a whole number of small firms on the eastern shore of Nova Scotia, was approved outside the program criteria. The ACOA offices in Atlantic Canada did not do the proper evaluation of the project.
Where is the accountability, I will ask my friend opposite. Where is the accountability in a system like that? Mr. Speaker, if you are asking for examples, or if you want to put forward examples of technical account-
November 26, 1990

ability or strengthening the laws, perhaps this bill addresses them.
The true question that has to be answered is why is this government not accountable for the way it spends the money of the people of Canada? An example would be the NSC Diesel fiasco for which the minister should have resigned and for which there should have been a full and complete police investigation. Perhaps we will have that yet.
There are a couple of points that need to be raised concerning this piece of legislation. I want to speak to some specific issues. I am going to start off at the back end of the bill and work my way forward. I want to talk about clause 40.
Clause 40 causes me great concern. We have a history in this country of equalization and of understanding that the country cannot be run as a business. It has to be run as a nation.
In order to run a country as vast and as great as Canada and have equity put in the system, it sometimes costs money. Sometimes, Mr. Speaker, you have to invest in infrastructure and admit that there is a cost for producing equity in this country, no matter where you live.
Mr. Speaker, if you live in Atlantic Canada you still have the right for quality health care. If you live in British Columbia, you should still have access to post-secondary educational institutions. We have entrenched in our Constitution the great liberal principle of equalization. It is there. It is what has made the country great.
Clause 40 tampers with the right of this Parliament to debate fundamental changes and directions in dealing with some Crown corporations.
I want to quote what it is going to do. Clause 40 effectively is going to do the following. It would effectively require commercial Crown corporations, those listed in Schedule III, Part II of the FAA, which operate in a competitive environment and not ordinarily dependent on appropriations for operating purposes, to incorporate dividend planning in its annual corporate plan.
In itself, that does not seem like a bad idea. If it is making money, it should put in its corporate plan that it expects to make money, and account for those revenues.
Government Orders
The bill goes a little further and says that the Governor in Council would be empowered to set, waive or vary dividend payments for any schedule Crown corporation.
There is something fundamentally wrong here. What happens if, by Order in Council-which means a cabinet decision-it decides to have incredible user fees or a very high dividend from a Crown corporation like Ports Canada. This would decrease the effectiveness of Ports Canada to be a competitive alternative to ports on the U.S. seaboard.
Look at the port of Halifax.
The Port of Halifax is responsible for nearly $750 million worth of activity in the economy of Atlantic Canada and, more particularly, in the Halifax-Dart-mouth area. Ports Canada is fighting for its life against subsidized activity from the port of New York and from rail lines like the D and H, which Canadian Pacific recently acquired. It will be able to draw goods currently destined for the central Canadian market away from Canadian ports and draw them in through the U.S. and up through the Atlantic Seaboard with a line like D and H.
That Crown corporation is there for a reason. That Crown corporation is there because previous governments have decided that the ports of Canada were a national resource that should be operated by a national government. This government has changed all that. As I said a little earlier, the government does not understand. It thinks that everything has to turn a profit and, if it does not, it is bad and it has to be dismantled and thrown out.
We have seen what a few years of that kind of policy has done. This country has never, ever, faced the crossroads of confidence that it faces today, because this government does not understand national unity and it does not understand the important role of national infrastructuring in keeping the country together.
The Port of Halifax is facing incredible competition from the ports in New York and New Jersey. There is no question that when the inter-state trade commission of the United States was examining the application by the Canadian Pacific Railway to acquire the bankrupt D and H line, which will be able to take goods right from the Port of Halifax straight up to the Quebec border, a

short-cut route for Canada-destined goods to get in through the United States, one of the largest shippers going into the Port of Halifax with containerized traffic indicated that it supported this application. It gave it an alternate and cheaper route for cargo going to the central part of Canada.
What does the Canadian government do? It forgets about the mandate of Canada Ports Corporation and, in the last budget, demanded that there be a dividend paid. This, at the very time that the people who are running the Port of Halifax have been doing everything but lying in the middle of the Macdonald Bridge and screaming to get the attention of the government that it is going to lose its competitive edge in trying to attract or keep container-based traffic going to the central part of Canada.
What does the government do? It forgets the mandate. It does not come to Parliament. It says in a budget that Ports Canada is going to have to pay a dividend. It forgets that it is there to do a job. It takes the money that Ports Canada needs to upgrade facilities, such as those at the Port of Halifax, and it says it has to be given to the government as a profit. The government takes the ability of the Port of Halifax and other ports to plan properly and, when they are efficient and make money, to have that money in reserve to reinvest.
I read here in Clause 40 of the bill that that may not be the case. The dividends that will be forced upon some of these Crown coqrorations can be made by a bunch of the guys and a few of the ladies who are on the opposite side, in the Cabinet, sitting down and deciding: "Well, I guess we blew it again. Before long, the debate that should take place in the House about the fundamental change in direction and philosophy of those Crown corporations will be muted and the government will be able, by that simple tool of Order in Council, that undemocratic tool, perhaps to dismantle even more of the national infrastructure and to do even more damage, not just to the economy of regions such as Atlantic Canada, but also to national unity. These are the underpinnings of national unity and anybody opposite who thinks they are not is crazy.
There are one or two other things I want to deal with. One of these, my colleague from Cape Breton Highlands-Canso dealt with and it is not a small issue. I hope that there are a whole lot of people out there watching, who have faith in their local fire departments. I hope that they are watching us as we speak.
I think it is Clause 6 which deals with user fees. Mr. Speaker, the government is absolutely crazed. It says: "Turn a profit, turn a profit, turn a profit." It does not matter what it shuts down, just turn a profit.
Let us not forget that it raised more personal income tax, I think 24 per cent or 27 per cent more, in the first half of this year than last year. By God, it is milking taxes out of us like we are a cow, an engorged cow. It just squeezes, squeezes, squeezes. It gets more and more cash. That is all it wants. It is so ashamed of what it has done on taxation that it has to find new ways to tax, and a tax is a tax is a tax. No matter how it takes it from someone's pocket, it is still taking it. But, it is dealing with something pretty dangerous here in user fees.
In 1986 the government changed the Telecommunications Act. The minister at the time was the former member for Kingston and the Islands, a former Cape Bretoner. I read the debates. There was a great debate, even in the Tory caucus, and the debate still goes on. It tells me that there are still a few people over there who are close to their constituents, not many, but a few. The minister at the time in the debate answered a question from the then member from South West Nova, who is now sitting in the other place as a senator. He was defeated by a Liberal, like most of those people were in Atlantic Canada at least. She said in response to a question from the former member from South West Nova that volunteer fire departments would be exempted. I do not have to embellish it. It is right there in the record. She said they would be exempted from those new licence fees.
What did the government do? It waited until it got another term in government and then it nailed the very organizations in communities, the people of which give of their time freely and risk their life and limb and security to ensure that the public safety and security is being looked after. I am talking about volunteer firemen,

for goodness sake. What did it do? This government, to milk a few more dollars, has gone after volunteer fire departments with unconscionable licence fees. Volunteer fire departments are not Liberal, Tories or NDPers. They are people in the communities and they feel very diminished. The minister opposite is nodding, and I hope he can tell his colleagues in cabinet that they should change this foolishness.
On user fees, the government would even hit volunteer fire departments. This means that in some cases there is over a 1000 per cent increase in the fee. A volunteer fire department, whether in Eastern Passage in my riding, or in any other ridings all over the country, has to raise its money. It gets a little bit of a fee from the municipality, but it has to hold bean suppers and fall fairs so that it can purchase equipment to protect the people in the community. What the government does is say work a little harder because it is going to charge a licence fee for every piece of communications equipment they have, not just one fee to cover the fire department, every single fee.
We started a petition drive. Every fire department in the country that I have been in touch with has indicated that these fees are not only regressive, but that they have been misled. In 1986, a very honourable member, the former member for Kingston and the Islands, said, as reported in Hansard, that the volunteer fire departments would be exempt. Again, because of user fees, the government thinks it can go in because there is nothing sacred. It does not matter if there is a fire department in some far-flung reach of this great nation that may have to forgo purchasing a new piece of equipment. Do not forget that they do not have bank accounts. They have to raise their money. Mostly, volunteer fire departments are in poor municipalities. These people are doing their part. For God's sake, the least the government can do with user fees is keep its hands out of their pockets.
I have talked to members opposite who have said the same thing. If there is one thing that the government could do to show that it has a little bit of compassion and understands how the country operates and the important contribution of volunteers like firemen and firewomen right across the country, is to say it made a mistake. It should live by the word and the commitment of the
Government Orders
former Minister of Communications and withdraw those fees. That is what it should do.
Every fireman, fire department or individual watching this tonight should write to their member of Parliament and tell them that. More particularly, they should write to the ministers on the front benches. It is one of those small things when you talk about user fees. It is easy to say it will only cost a few bucks. But when looking at the potential damage to get that few extra bucks, it could be a little bit more financially responsible and ingenious on that side of the House. The few dollars the government will pick up on that may result in a slower response to an emergency in a community. It should withdraw the fee. That is why I have a little bit of a problem with the user fees.
I used to think that democracy worked in a certain way, that no matter if a government came in with a piece of legislation, if it saw that for whatever reason there was a flaw in it, it would change it. The government has developed a siege mentality when it comes to this type of initiative and it simply will not do it.
We on this side of the House are going to continue. I will be up every day, if I have to, presenting petitions from volunteer fire departments until the government comes to its senses and realizes there are certain things that cannot be touched and cannot be milked from the country because of its financial irresponsibility and mismanagement.
The last thing deals with transportation and infrastructure generally, user fees again. We have seen the government, with its quest for the bottom line, dismantle many pieces of the national infrastructure. Well, we do not all live in a Toronto, or Hamilton, or Vancouver, or even Halifax. Some of us have to live in other beautiful parts of the country where we do not perhaps have infrastructure that supports itself.
I talked a little bit earlier about the principle of equalization. It is enshrined in our Constitution-it is there. It means that the government, the people in the country, believe that we have to make level playing-fields, that there is a cost in keeping this nation together. It does not mean that we squander our money, but it

Government Orders
means that we recognize that there is a cost and that we budget for it.
The government is now toying with full recovery fees, full implementation of cost recovery in the air transportation sector. Well, Mr. Speaker, do you know what that means? If we want to talk about destroying national unity, here is what it means. I am reading from a document from Air Nova in Atlantic Canada. I hope you will be a little patient because this is pretty important. It states that under full implementation of cost recovery, Halifax will be the most expensive of the nine major airports in the country. For example, a Dash-8 landing in Halifax will have to pay a fee of $121.60. The same Dash-8 landing in Vancouver, because it is a larger airport with more traffic, pays $37.60. A Boeing 747 landing in Halifax will cost $2,675.20. The same 747 landing in Toronto is $616.
This government has gone bonkers. It is going to try to implement full user fees, forgetting the fact that this is a regional economy, that we have many regions here, and it is going to try to take the levelling effect out of many of the user fees that we have in this country. It is going to pull another spike out of the track of national unity. Eventually, it will have Canadians so distraught at the way it has mismanaged us that, when it comes to the next great national unity debate, it will be hard to muster the forces in many parts of the country because of this government's financial mismanagement plan.
I could speak for days about what the government is doing, but suffice it to say that I will be on my feet again to complete my speech under another piece of legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to what was said by the hon. member for Dartmouth. I had trouble accepting some of the points he raised, especially when he claimed that the Government of Canada should spend certain amounts of money and transfer amounts hither and thither. My impression is that he would want the government to do all this without considering its ability to pay or the taxpayers' ability to pay.
Mr. Speaker, I may remind the hon. member that Canada has a very substantial cumulative deficit which we must start paying off as soon as possible. If we don't, and if we don't succeed in putting into place various ways to control government spending and bring down the
deficit, the equalization principle mentioned by the hon. member will be a commitment this government will no longer be able to meet because it will not have the money to do so. There will not be enough money to do this, and Canadians of course will not have the ability to pay.
To get back to his comment on user fees, I think the hon. member would agree that a great deal can be done in this area. Obviously, the government must try to recover the costs of infrastructures, whether we are talking about marine facilities, airports or other areas where it is entirely normal that users should pay a certain amount of money.
We can question the amounts, we can question the tariffs and we can question the principle according to which the prices are set. However, I think the principle that users should contribute to the cost of infrastructures put in place by taxpayers is a universally recognized principle that should help, on the basis of revenue the government will raise, to absorb the costs of these infrastructures and maintain them in proper condition.
So I think the hon. member should have the honesty and common sense to admit that the principle of charging users certain amounts for the infrastructures made available to them by taxpayers is a fair principle and a sound one, and aside from the amounts to be charged and the tariffs to be set, I think the hon. member will agree that the principle of charging users certain amounts for public infrastructures should be acknowledged and maintained.

I certainly do realize that in some cases the government has to be efficient. Let us be fair. This government came into office and all was going to be wonderful in la-la land the day after it got in. It is finding out that that is not the easiest thing to do.
Six years later and it is worse.

Six years later is much worse, as my colleague for Kingston and the Islands said.
The member opposite wants to talk about fairness. I will give him a little lesson from his own books about fairness. We witnessed on Friday the government coming in, saying that first of all it needed more money and it
November 26, 1990

was going to trim bucks from all over the place, but it was going to be fair.
I want to tell you how fair they are going to be, Mr. Speaker. They came into the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency, that quasi accountable agency that I referred to earlier, and do you know what the government did? It took about $650,000 from administration. Okay. Maybe it is going to have to do a little better with a little less money.
The government went over to the Western Diversification Fund which is the agency to deliver regional development in the west, like ACOA is the agency to deliver regional development to business and business assistance in the east. What did it do? It took $20 million in deferred grants and contributions from ACOA and did not take one penny in deferred grants and contributions from the Western Diversification Fund.
What the member opposite has to understand is that you cannot go about abusing the trust and misusing the resources that this country has and treat one part of your family differently than another part of your family. If the cuts are to be effected, then it should have effected it across the board. There should not be one member from Atlantic Canada on the Tory benches, not one member opposite who agrees that any part of the country, be it east or west, should suffer more under government cuts.
Do you know what they are saying opposite, Mr. Speaker? A great nationalist that I am, I believe everybody in this country should be treated equally. I guess I squeal a little bit when I see people from my part of the country who had the good sense to vote Liberal getting the boot from this government every time it comes in with its fiscal knife.
Howard is laughing.
Howard is laughing at us.

The member for Halifax West is laughing. But the member for Halifax West also laughed when I raised in the House the problems about the decreased competitiveness for the port of Halifax. He also laughed when we held up the strike-breaking legislation that his government brought in against the ships' crews and he also laughed when our party sup-
Govemment Orders
ported the end of a wage inequity through regional rates of pay for dockyard workers. That member will be laughing on the other side of his face the next time the electors have a chance to deal with him.
That's right.

Mr. Speaker, I listened to my colleague for Dartmouth with a great deal of interest. I think he has expressed quite well the plight in which this government has placed Atlantic Canada. It is absolutely devastating to our economy, this idea of complete cost recovery of all government expenditures.
I fully expect that this is not the end of it. I think we have an awful lot of user pay without it being designated as user pay. One example of this is in small craft harbours where this government is ignoring the plight of the fishermen in allowing the wharves which the fishermen need so desperately to fall into disrepair. Also, they are not doing any dredging in the small harbours.
That is not only a question of hurting the fishing industry, but it is also a question of allowing the silt to fill in the mouths of the harbours so that in rough weather fishermen cannot re-enter their harbours. They are in the position of being at risk of their lives out in the Atlantic Ocean.
Also, this government is actually diverting business away from the ports of Halifax and Saint John by refusing to put into place the repairs to infrastructure needed for Canadian National and actually encouraging Canadian cargo to be shipped into New York and transported by train from New York to Montreal and Toronto.
I would like to ask the hon. member, because he has spoken about this often, to comment on these and give us his interpretation as to whether these are as damaging to Atlantic Canada as I believe or whether I am being an alarmist in this regard.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague from Cape Breton-The Sydneys, somebody who has stood up over and over again not just for the people of his riding but for all the people of Atlantic Canada and for a vision of this country where equality of opportunity exists no matter where you live.

November 26, 1990
Government Orders
In response, I think this government has no sense of where it is going. It rules from the centre. It rules for the centre and rules to where the numbers are at. That means that if you can withdraw fiscal support to create a level playing field in places like Atlantic Canada, so be it. If it means that you can pit one part of Canada, east against west, you do it because all the Conservatives are concerned about is pleasing their buddies down on Bay Street and they do not know the first thing about national unity or the role that national infrastructure like railways, ports and small craft harbours play in keeping this great country together.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to have an opportunity to participate in this debate today because I noticed the President of the Treasury Board on his hind legs this morning telling us about the virtues of Bill C-91. I thought that it was appropriate to indicate some of the disasters.
I note that the bill is an act to amend the Financial Administration Act. Really, for this government to introduce a bill that has to do with good administration was an incredible sight. We had the minister standing there telling us how much more efficient this bill was going to make the government. Well, anything would be an improvement. There is no doubt about that. I have grave doubts though. When the minister talks about efficiency, he talks about nothing more than gouging and screwing tax dollars out of Canadians, which this government has shown itself to be so good at.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: Be positive. Don't be so mean spirited.

The parliamentary secretary suggests that perhaps I am being mean spirited. I suggest that is not the case. The minister beamed and smiled his way through his presentation. He did very well, considering the material he had to work with. I suggest that what we have to do with this bill is have a good long look at it and look at the very bad administration that Canadians have been treated to under this government.
I want to turn to the supplementary estimates which the minister tabled the other day because I think they reveal something of the ability of this government to administer-
Is this a point of privilege or debate?

If the hon. member listens for a moment, I think he will enjoy these comments. Page 32 of the supplementary estimates has some of the costs of the goods and services tax which this government is applying to Canadians. It is establishing a goods and services tax consumer information office. If you do a little arithmetic, Mr. Speaker, not complicated, a little arithmetic, you can see that they are hiring 20 new people, 20 person years are authorized. If you divide that into the amount of money for personnel that is shown in the estimates you get an average salary of $54,150 per annum for those individuals. That sounds a little high, but I will come back to that.
If we turn to page 84 the hon. member will see that in the Department of National Revenue, Customs and Excise, 1,163 lucky Canadians are going to be hired as tax police to enforce the new goods and services tax at an average salary according to these estimates of $41,490. You will notice that is down a little from the previous group that is working with the corporations.
Then if you look across the page you will see in the Taxation Division of National Revenue they are preparing and planning for pre-payment of the tax credits. In other words, this is the group that hands the money out to Canadians that we are all supposed to be so thankful for. The average salary of the 642 people being hired in that department is $33,124. Why would it be so much lower for the individuals who are going to pay out the revenue to Canadians, the great bonanza that they are getting back, than for the ones who are going to gouge and screw the tax out of Canadians? I know why. The government is more interested in getting the money than it is in paying it out. Why pay someone a lot of money to give money back to Canadians? Pay it to get it out of them. That is the priority of this government. That is what it means about better administration under the Financial Administration Act.
If that is not enough to convince the hon. member, he can turn to page 100 of the estimates. There we have the people who are actually going to send the cheques. "Preparation and planning for the prepayment of the GST credit to taxpayers", that is the people who actually write the cheques, I presume, in the Supply and Services Department, since that is where cheques are issued. The average salary there is the lowest yet. They are expecting to hire 45 people for this work at an average salary of
November 26, 1990

$31,471. In other words, who are the highest paid in this group? The ones who are advising the corporations, the ones who are in the Consumer and Corporate Affairs Department to advise the corporations, presumably, on how to make their tax payments most efficiently. They are being paid the most. Then we go to the Department of National Revenue where they actually go around and tax police and gouge Canadians for their money. They are going to be paid the second highest. The ones who make the refunds are the lowest paid on the totem pole.
I ask the hon. member to ask the minister for details on this. I am sure the minister would be more than happy to fill him in on how many senior bureaucrats are going to be hired at higher salaries in the upper end of the Consumer and Corporate Affairs Department. Take a look at the figures. I urge the hon. member to read the Supplementary Estimates. Perhaps he will find that he agrees with my analysis of this situation and will realize that when the President of the Treasury Board talks about better administration, what he is talking about is screwing more money out of Canadians.
I was happy to receive a press release recently from business leaders. This came from the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association and the Business Council. I know that the minister got a copy too. These business leaders all called on Ottawa and the provinces to curb spending. These people were simply appalled at this government's spending record, its out-of-control budget deficits, its inability to do anything effectively to control the deficit.
Some of these people may like the GST, but the bulk of the small businessmen who I know in Canada are dead set against this tax. The hon. member knows that too. If he were doing his job, he would be filing petitions from his constituents who are signing them by the hundred and who are, I have no doubt, opposing this tax. He should not sit there worrying about whether these people are opposed to the GST. They are opposed to the tax. Over 80 per cent of the population is opposed to this tax. I will give that fact to the hon. member. If he were listening to the 80 per cent of Canadians who are, he would be up voting against this tax, and sitting on this side of the House with his former colleagues who have
Government Orders
had the good sense to get out of the Progressive Conservative Party and sit on this side of the House.
I turn to the allegation of the minister this morning that this bill is supposed to be good for Canadians. He said that it would be good for Canada because it would make the government more efficient. I want to look at some of the evidence of the government's efficiency over the past few years. I have a calculation that I did from the Public Accounts of Canada. I thought that we might usefully see what kind of increases in taxes Canadians have had to face in the last few years.
Doing a year-on-year comparison of the increases in revenue, I was able to determine that from 1984-85, or in the 1985 financial year, there was a 10 per cent increase in revenue in the Government of Canada. 1985 was the first big Tory year. It was the first year after that disastrous election in 1984 that crippled the Canadian economy.
I can remember the Diefenbaker government. I remember and I am sure hon. members opposite will agree with me that it was probably the worst government Canada had ever had up until that time. Everyone acknowledges that the Diefenbaker government was a complete disaster for Canada.
The only one that I can imagine is worse is the present one. These figures bear that out. For 1984-1985 revenue increased 10 per cent, that is 1985 over 1984; the next year, an 8 per cent increase; the next year, 11 per cent; the next year, a 13 per cent increase; the next year, 6 per cent; and this year, 1990 over 1989, it is projected at 9 per cent.
That is the kind of revenue increases we have had under this government. We have indicated it has increased taxes over 31 times, and now think what it is going to be like under the GST. Think what it will be like under the GST. And here the minister is concerned about efficiency-
You'll have no room on your credit card.

The hon. member says he has no room on the credit card. That is because the government has failed to live up to its responsibilities and its promises. That is the reason for it, and he knows it, and he should get this government out at the earliest opportunity.

Government Orders
Now we could turn to the percentage change in personal income tax and corporate tax revenue. Let us look at the personal income tax changes over this period, that is the amount of revenue the government derived from that source. In 1984-1985, that is the 1985 year over 1984, revenue from personal income taxes went up 8 per cent; the next year, 12 per cent; the next year, 14 per cent; the next year, 19 per cent-19 per cent in one year, Mr. Speaker. In 1989 over 1988 we have the big decrease. It only went up by 2 per cent.
Guess what? Maybe there was an election. Maybe it reduced taxes because there was an election. Is that possible? I would not have thought this government would be that politically motivated, yet it appears that is what might have happened. From 1989 to 1990, that is this year over last year, because of the tax increases and the recent budget, 12 per cent. Is that not an extraordinary story: 8, 12, 14, 19, election year 2, and the next year 12. That is what this government has been doing to Canadians. It has been fiddling around with the public accounts, the taxes, and so on, in order to make things easy for Canadians when it is time to re-elect it but dam difficult in all the years in between. That is what has been going on.
The corporate tax increases reflect a similar pattern but not the same. The first year, 1985 over 1984, there was a 28 per cent increase. It must have been a profitable year for the corporations. The next year it was 2 per cent; the next year, 7 per cent; the next year, 10 per cent; the next year, the election one, 7 per cent; the next one, 11 per cent. Modest increases by comparison. Compound them and I will bet you will find they are lower, and indeed all the figures suggest exactly that.
What this government means by saying that it wants to make financial administration of the government more efficient is that it wants to get more money out of Canadians for more things. You can look at the act. You will see that it applies interest on all kinds of obligations that citizens have to the government. It enables the government to use a collection agency so it will be more efficient in collecting money from Canadians and in collecting arrears of taxes. That is the purpose of this bill. Let us not kid around.
While we will say that some of the changes are quite laudable and probably worth while, the fact is this government is a real pro when it comes to squeezing
money out of Canadians and failing to deliver on the return side.
The other thing I thought was important and interesting as I perused this little bill the government has introduced was the fact that it left something out. We all know that this government has shown repeated, continuous contempt for this institution. It is showing it in the other place this very day, I have no doubt. I do not know what has happened down there this afternoon, but I am sure that the Conservative majority and its puppet, the Speaker, is busy doing what it can to deprive the opposition in that House of an opportunity to debate this bill. I suggest that what is going on there is another indication of the contempt this government shows for Parliament.
We saw it before because of course government members got into a mess when they called Parliament back after the 1989 election for two weeks and then decided that rather than face the music in this House they would help themselves to the public money by Governor General's special warrants. They abused these warrants in a way they had never been used before in Canada, by grabbing billions of dollars out of the public Treasury by warrant between sessions of Parliament, something that had never happened in this country before on anything like that scale and which I submit- and I submitted it at the time-was entirely improper, so much so that I felt I should-
You lost the debate.

Yes, I did, because I was overruled by a large majority in this House. That is why I lost this debate; not because there was any element of fairness. The Speaker said that he would not rule on the issue.
When it was raised in committee, the Conservative majority in the committee silenced the issue very promptly. The hon. member for Halifax West was there. He ranted and raved. He said that I was being partisan in raising the issue. It was a completely improper use of the authority granted to cabinet and to the Governor General under the Financial Administration Act, this very Act that we are now seeking to amend.
Wonderful thing. Mr. Speaker, you look through this Act in vain for any change to the provision relating to the use of Governor General special warrants. I would have thought the government might want to put some restriction on its future misconduct in this field, because I
November 26, 1990

suspect we are about to see its misuse again before too long in spite of the grumbles from the hon. member for Halifax West.
I know this subject is a sore point with him. I believe he has some considerable experience in legal matters. I am sure he understands perfectly the arguments that I made in respect of those Governor General's warrants. I expect he agrees with every argument I made that in fact there was a flagrant abuse by the government of the use of those means of obtaining public money. It helped itself to the Treasury in a way that was completely unprecedented and wrong.
I introduced a private member's bill, Bill C-211, which sought to restrict the use of Governor General's special warrants. That bill is still sitting on the Order Paper. I am optimistic, as I am sure Your Honour is, that sooner or later it will be drawn in the famous draw that takes place every few weeks in Private Members' Business. Maybe we will get to discuss it in this House some day.
In the meantime, I would have thought that the government might have incorporated my amendment, or something like it, in Bill C-91. I went through the bill and I was dismayed to see not a word or mention of any change to section 30 of the Financial Administration Act, which might have corrected these bad habits on the part of the government.
It could easily have made it unlawful for it to do what I submit is improper and unlawful, that is, to abuse these warrants the way it has. Yet the amendment is not there.
I would invite the hon. member for Halifax West, who I know agrees with me in this regard, to raise this matter in caucus on Wednesday morning and see if he cannot get the minister to agree to an amendment to Bill C-91 so that we can fix this mess up now and not have a recurrence of the disastrous events of early 1989.
I can say that if the minister is worried about the amendment to the bill, I would be happy to have my bill read for the second time, by unanimous consent, and referred to the legislative committee with Bill C-91. The amendment could be incorporated into the bill. I do not want to claim pride of authorship. I am not worried about that. I just want the law fixed.
Government Orders
I know hon. members opposite would be more than happy to ensure that their government did not act improperly or wrongly again, because it must have been a very embarrassing day for the hon. member for Halifax West and others to have to vote with the government when the government had acted with such obvious [DOT]impropriety.
I submit what we have in this case is a bill that the government has introduced with one purpose in mind: To get more money from you, from me, and from the Canadian taxpayer. What it wants to be able to do-and the minister said it this morning-is collect money more efficiently. It wants to be able to manage the accounts of Canada more efficiently.
He made some reference to the fact that this would help the Auditor General and made a few other what I could only describe as pious utterances, to try to make the bill more palatable. It really is-and I think a quick glance through the provisions of the bill indicates that- an attempt to get more money out of Canadians in a faster, more direct, and perhaps more simple manner for the government.
I submit that while perhaps that is a laudable aim, it is not particularly a fair one for Canadians. We will want to examine the provisions of this bill on a clause by clause basis when the bill gets referred to the legislative committee.
I think the other part of the equation that I did not mention earlier is important. I talked about the increase in revenue, but I neglected to talk about the increase in expenditures. The businessmen who issued the communique I referred to a moment ago, the joint statement on the national economy from the Chamber of Commerce, among others, mentioned that spending was out of control. I have some figures to show just how much spending went up in the course of time.
The only reason I did not mention them was because the spending did not go up as fast as the revenue did. The revenue increases have been fairly astronomic, as the House has heard. Expenditures were a little more modest. I say a little more modest: 13 per cent the first year, 1 per cent the next, 4 per cent, 7 per cent, 5 per cent, and 7 per cent. So, you can hear, Mr. Speaker, that they are lower than the revenue.

Adjournment Debate
The revenue, of course, is the taxes we are all paying, but it did not cut-
What was it for the election year?

No, no. It was 7 per cent the year before. The hon. member will be glad to know it was one of the highest.
I should also tell the hon. member that the national debt increased fairly significantly throughout this year. In fact we all know it doubled; 22 per cent in the first year, 16 per in the second, 12 per cent in the third, 10 per cent in the fourth, 9.9 per cent in the fifth, and 8.8 per cent in the sixth.
It is getting smaller.

It is getting smaller, yes. As the hon. member says it is getting smaller. The increase is getting smaller because the debt is so much bigger. If the hon. member would study the figures sometime, he would find that what this government has done is allow the national debt to increase at a record pace in spite of all the phoney claims to the contrary. The idea that the operating budget is in surplus, what nonsense. You do not run an office and not pay the rent. This government is trying to claim it has a surplus because it is running the office and it is not paying the rent. It has to pay the rent. Canadians are having to pay the rent. This bill is one more indication of the government's desire to gouge and screw the Canadian taxpayer. We object to it.

Mr. Speaker, I was interested in my colleague's comments regarding the debt and the deficit. We do know how the debt has grown in the last six years. Not only has it grown, but the percentage of the debt that is being financed abroad has grown.
In 1984, when this government took office, the debt was around $170 billion and about 17 per cent of Treasury bonds were financed outside the country. Now the debt is $380 billion and 37 per cent of the debt is being financed outside the country.
It would be nice to have free trade with the Americans where we would be on an even footing. Of course interest rates are now 500 basis points higher than the Americans. Before the free trade agreement we could say: "If you are going to do business in Canada you have to manufacture in Canada". The free trade agreement did away with that, so it now seems that there is a haemorrhaging of businesses away from Canada into the
United States. There is really very little we can do because of the government's financial fiasco other than bring out new financial policies, which this government refuses to do.
Has the hon. member, as a member from southern Ontario, experienced this trend of businesses leaving Canada and going to the United States as a result of the disastrous financial policies of this government?

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to respond to my very learned and distinguished colleague from Cape Breton-The Sydneys.
I want to confirm that in fact there have been closures of businesses in my riding. I know of two that closed for the sole purpose of moving to the United States. There have been extensive lay-offs, particularly in the last few weeks as the recession for which the government claims credit-it claims it created it as a result of its policies- takes hold on the Canadian economy, throwing Canadians out of work.
On the other side of the coin, which my hon. friend mentioned, was the difficulty we face in borrowing abroad and the significant borrowings we have. Of course the higher the government deficit is, the more it drives Canadian investment out of Canada. Canadian companies cannot get capital on the markets at a reasonable rate, so they are forced to go and borrow abroad, which means we have more foreign investment in Canada and more Canadian industries being sold.
When this government said that Canada was open for business again, it really meant Canada is up for sale again. That is what it was talking about.

15, regarding a barge carrying three million gallons of bunker oil. At that time it was projected to travel through the Gulf Islands of my riding and into the waters of Saanich Inlet, on which a number of people are working hard to have become a federal marine reserve park. My question related to the regulatory vacuum that existed in respect of oil barges and tanker traffic in that area.
I want to take the opportunity now to expand on that because we have, since that question was asked and the government responded, received the report from the public review panel on tanker safety, marine spills and the response capability. This panel was appointed on June 9, 1989 by the Prime Minister. The report's short name is the Brander-Smith report. I would like to take the opportunity to highlight some of the report's findings, because they are quite critical and point out some of the regulatory vacuum which I highlighted in my question of last May.
One of the panel's major findings was that the capability to respond effectively to a spill of any significant magnitude did not presently exist anywhere in Canada. This shows the reality of the situation.
Another finding was that a much greater volume of oil enters the marine environment as a result of routine tanker operations such as loading, offloading, tank washings, and waste water discharges than as a result of accidents. Almost all of these operational skills can be avoided. Only 8 per cent of the oil tankers operating world-wide have double hulls or bottoms. Of Canada's 31 tankers, only one is double hulled and ice-reinforced.
Over all, foreign tankers pose a much greater threat to our shores than domestic tankers. Almost one-quarter of the foreign tankers inspected by the Canadian Coast Guard in the Atlantic region, over an 18-month period ending December 31, 1989, were found to be defective. There is a requirement, because Canada is a signatory to an international agreement, that Canada inspect one-quarter of the foreign tankers. Only 8 per cent of those foreign tankers are inspected, because there is not the capacity to inspect the others.
I read in The Toronto Star of November 24 about an incident which occurred just off our Atlantic coast. I think it shows the mindset of some of the members of
Adjournment Debate
the Department of Transport. We are talking about a major spill off the coast of Nova Scotia, and a Transport Canada spokesperson said that it was really out of our jurisdiction because the spill occurred in international waters and it was a foreign tanker, a Norwegian ship.
"It is really out of our jurisdiction" is almost like the "it is not my department" kind of response which I find and I think all members of this House find very irritating when we have to deal with any bureaucracy. It is our department, it is our jurisdiction, because we all live on one planet and it is in our interest that this issue is looked at. I know that the government is trying to use shrinking resources in order to do a job, but we have to reassess our priorities to make certain that people really understand what the danger is. When we are told that there is no capability to respond effectively in the case of any major spill, that is a pretty significant finding.
I would like to point out some other findings. There is also a glaring need to standardize and upgrade dockside chemical loading and offloading requirements, as well as the design, construction, and inspection of chemical tankers and barges.
I think this is the key recommendation or the key finding. In my riding, the Coast Guard receives a lot of criticism for its inability to respond. This finding is that the Coast Guard is seriously under-resourced and cannot provide for the level of monitoring, inspection and surveillance required to adequately protect our waters.
The people who work for the Coast Guard are probably doing their best but they are just not given adequate resources. I think it is up to the Minister of Transport to go to cabinet and say, "In order to do our job properly, we have to have these resources".
I will quote from the report. I think it is important that I get this right.
The Coast Guard's investigative and prosecution efforts are seriously inadequate and do little to deter polluters. Indeed, the chances of polluters being caught are small; of being caught and prosecuted even smaller. If polluters are prosecuted, the chances of being found guilty are minuscule and, if found guilty, fines are paltiy. In the few instances where prosecutions are attempted and prove successful, fines are unacceptably meagre: between 1979 and 1988, the average fine under the Canada Shipping Act was $4,700.
That is hardly a deterrent.

November 26, 1990
Adjournment Debate
Mr. Speaker, you are giving me the sign that I have only one minute left. There is a lot more I could say on this. What the government has to do is to start implementing these recommendations. The regulatory vacuum that exists is frightening for anybody who cares about the environment; anybody who lives on the coast line; anybody who has a business that depends on a pristine marine environment. That is a lot of people. We have to be able to integrate our economy and our environment. We have to start putting sufficient resources into protection of our environment so that the environment is protected.

speakeroldname: Mr. Dave Worthy (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs) and Minister of State (Finance)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Finance); Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member for Saanich-Gulf Islands. I know she is extremely serious in her questioning, as she should be when it comes to the environment, especially to something that could permanently damage and irrevocably harm any part of our environment. She has to be especially serious because of the coast line in the area in which she lives. As she points out, it is the job of all parties to be questioning and critical. It is the government's job to respond, and I will try to do that now.
Sharing the hon. member's concern, as all of us do, our Prime Minister announced the Public Review Panel on Tanker Safety and Marine Spill Response Capability in June of 1989. This was the David Brander-Smith report. It was released November 2 of this year and it is far-reaching. The recommendations have been accepted by the department and will assist in the improvement of Canada's spill response capability.
Some of the initial actions now under way by the Coast Guard include the developing of barge regulations and the planning for the improvement and upgrading of equipment.
In addition, the Canadian Coast Guard has a number of contingency plans in place to attempt to deal with ship or barge source oil spills. The master plan is the National Marine Emergency Plan which covers all Canadian waters. On the west coast, this is supplemented by the Western Region Contingency Plan.
Furthermore, should a spill impact on boundary waters, the Canada-United States Joint Marine Pollution Contingency Plan would be invoked. This calls for the combined Canada-U.S. pollution countermeasure response. These contingency plans are exercised, of course, with our American colleagues on a regular basis.
In terms of resources, the Canadian Coast Guard has major pollution countermeasures equipment depots at Victoria, Vancouver and Prince Rupert. A recent one has been established in Sandspit and another is being established at Ucluelet.
There are also a number of private sector resources that can be called upon. In addition, of course, Canada can call on the U.S. Coast Guard in case of emergency.
The Canadian Coast Guard monitoring vessel monitors Canada's traffic movements on Canada's coast on a continuous basis and provides a reporting point for spills of oil or noxious substances. While my comments have been specific to the hon. member's region, needless to say all regions of Canada are being upgraded and similarly equipped.
Mr. Brander-Smith's study was in depth and far reaching in its implications. The panel's hard work is greatly appreciated and, as the hon. member indicated, it will go a long way to improving our marine response capability if we in fact can follow up on it.
