Mr. Speaker, I want to make it quite clear to the hon. member that I am a very strong supporter of co-op housing and a very strong supporter of a continuing co-op housing program.
I know that the hon. member is aware that the federal government has been involved in a co-op housing program of one sort or another since the 1970s. In fact there have been three separate co-operative housing programs dating back to the 1970s. Each one has had different criteria, different aspects to it but all of those programs together have produced some 45,000 or more units of co-operative housing over the length of time there has been federal co-operative housing programs. Since 1985 when the current co-operative housing program was put into effect, over 13,000 units of co-op housing have been included and added to that total.
Back in 1985 the federal government, as you know, Mr. Speaker, and as the hon. member knows, conducted some consultations with respect to its housing policies in order to determine where we should go from that point. At that time there were consultations broadly held with the entire housing industry, all groups involved, including the co-op housing movement and everyone associated with it. Out of that came a consensus that the government would try from that point forward to target all of its housing dollars to those people in our country who were most in need of housing.
The hon. member is well aware that there are an awful lot of people in that category who are not being served today. In fact, about 1.2 million households in this country fall into that category.
The difficulty, as the hon. member is aware, is the fact that the co-operative housing program fact is not entirely targeted to low-income people. It is in fact, by definition, and by philosophy a program which is a mixture of incomes and therefore, as a result of that, is an exception to the government's housing policy targeting all housing funds to low-income people.
This housing program that was put into effect, being an ILM, an index-linked mortgage program, for five years was carried out in consultation with the co-op housing movement. It was to achieve some 5,000 units of co-op housing a year, but in fact failed to do that, not because there was any intention on the government to
not produce that amount of money, but because there was an agreement made to put $5 million a year into producing units of co-op housing. We were unable to achieve that target because of the differing real interest rates on ILM mortgages and because the subsidy per unit cost rose from $1,000 to over $3,000 per unit at the current time. We have been endeavouring through our consultation process and our evaluation process to come up with a new program and some new recommendations in good faith. I will be making those recommendations to cabinet before the end of the year. I can assure the hon. member that I am certain he will be pleased with the results of those recommendations.

Mr. Speaker, the issue that I continue to raise with the Minister of National Health and Welfare concerns ethics in biomedical research. When may clinical testing of drugs be done on humans and how should subjects be enrolled in the clinical study? Does it matter whether the sponsor of drug testing is a medical school, a hospital, a doctor's clinic or a medical establishment?
On November 5, Canadians saw on national television a revelation that Canadian subjects had been enrolled in a clinical trial of the drug HI-6, an antidote against nerve gas poison, sponsored by the Department of National Defence, without them being fully informed that the drug could cause cancer, apparently despite contraiy advice from the ministry of health.
Hence, my first question to the minister on November 6 was: "Could he explain why this study went ahead despite non-compliance with our Canadian ethical standards? Was he surprised and would he halt the study unless it reveals all known side effects to volunteers and thereby ensure informed consent?"
The minister in essence replied that in subsequent trials, that is during phase two, he will insist that a specific reference be made as to the possibility of carcinogenicity notwithstanding the fact that no direct evidence suggests the drug can cause cancer.
On November 7, I again posed a question to the minister. I challenged him to admit that the necessary tests for cancer in animals have not yet been done. I called to his attention that the drug is prohibited from
November 26, 1990

being manufactured in the United States because of danger to the employees and the community.
Earlier, during Question Period at that time, the Minister of National Defence had admitted that one ingredient used in the manufacturing of the drug is bis-chloromethyl ether, which is a known carcinogen, that is, it has cancer-causing properties.
The minister for health, in his reply, indicated that tests done in other jurisdictions showed the drug is safe. If one did not specifically test for cancer-causing properties of the drug and one did not have so-called purity data, that is the extent of chemical reactions during manufacturing, one takes the risk the carcinogenic ingredient could transmit its danger.
In fact, allowing such a practice would set a bad precedent for testing of new drugs for cancer in animals before trials in humans. To say that HI-6 could possibly cause cancer without animal data is meaningless and unethical.
On November 8, one of the subjects for the clinical trials was quoted in the press as having agreed to participate mainly because he was "broke" and he stayed in the study because he needed the money.
I therefore asked the minister whether enticing Canadians who are poor with extra dollars to serve as subjects is ethical. Examination of the consent form reveals some inconsistencies with respect to this matter. Page 3 of the form states: "Discontinuation from the study will involve no penalty", yet, page 4 states: "the subject will only receive percentage of the full fee-" unless the subject completes, "all aspects of the study."
Page 2 of the consent form alluded to one clinical study in Yugoslavia to sustain the claim that there were no untoward effects to date yet page 3 of the form alluded to "previous clinical studies", thereby suggesting more than one. My question is, why the discrepancy in numbers?
The form also indicates that the drug "may damage sperm cells which could result in birth defects." While advice was given to subjects "to practice contraception
Adjournment Debate
during the study and for 90 days following the study," no clear information was available as to possible damage that may occur as a consequence of cumulative doses as this particular study would allow.
I further challenged the minister why the clinical testing on humans should proceed before testing for cancer is done on animals. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I thought the government had the sequence backwards.
The issue before us is indeed most important. I would like to conclude by reading into the record of this debate a brief letter to the editor of The Globe and Mail, the issue of last November 11, from Dr. David Roy, Director of the Centre for Bioethics and Clinical Research at the Institute of Montreal. He writes:
Respect for human beings and the protection of their health and lives, dignity and rights have formed the core of the many codes and guidelines governing the ethics of research with human subjects since the Second World War. The Nuremberg code marks a turning point. It crystallized the essential characteristics of consent required to protect the autonomy of human beings in biomedical research.
Consent is not voluntary if people are seduced by money to submit themselves to potentially dangerous tests of new drugs. Consent to such tests is not adequately informed if those seduced to participate are not told about the effects previous tests of a new drug have had on animal and human bodies. Consent cannot be adequately informed if previous testing was insufficient to deliver reliable information about possible toxicity. Consent cannot be comprehending if warnings are couched in terms so vague they blind participants to the possible dangers of testing.
He continued:
It makes no difference whether the sponsor of drug testing is the medical establishment, a drug company, or the military-the ethics of research with human beings remains the same.
He concluded his letter:
We must not now, or ever, abandon the ethical progress we have made with and since Nuremberg.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, the HI-6 drug testing in question has failed to fully comply with the established ethical guidelines that now govern the conduct of biomedical research in human volunteers. Therefore, this particular study must be halted until the required animal studies for the concerns that I have raised have been done.
I trust and hope that this government will respond accordingly.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for raising this question during the adjournment debate and for giving me this opportunity to repeat the guidelines for testing new products.
I am sure you will understand, and I assume the hon. member is aware, that the Department of National Health and Welfare takes this very seriously. It does not take lightly the risks to human beings who test new products.
Obviously, Health and Welfare Canada considers the risks and must weigh the pros and cons, before it finally authorizes human testing.
In the case of HI-6, Health and Welfare analysed these aspects, and at the time it was concluded most emphatically, on the basis of the evidence, that its benefits as an antidote for organic phosphate gases outweighed the potential risk.
There have been allegations that it would be harder for a company than a department to reach that conclusion. Not so. In this particular case, the Department of National Defence had to conform to the same guidelines
and then some, before Health and Welfare Canada would allow this product to be tested.
Of course there is also the matter of compliance with the Food and Drugs Act and Regulations. Mr. Speaker, it has also been alleged that the regulations themselves are not strong enough. That is not the case. In fact, we are told the exact opposite is true. Often companies launch new products they are sure will be good for various diseases, including AIDS in one case. We heard a lot about this in connection with a drug for AIDS.
Mr. Speaker, I may add that the Department of National Health and Welfare has the authority under the Act. It is all very regulated.
There is also the ethical aspect, and I agree with the hon. member that it must be very strictly observed. Canada signed the Helsinki Convention. This aspect is very strictly enforced, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure that with the help of the hon. member, we will continue to ensure that our standards are the very highest and protect the health of Canadians who test these products.
